And rather than solving it, they just dump it on other people without any detail… I just don’t think they are aware enough to understand that the solution to all their problems is not Chuck Schumer. Subscribe to print for your office or home. “D on’t move, senior citizen coming down.” Jensen Huang put his hands on Elon Musk’s shoulders and hopped off the dais, rejoining Michael Dell, Satya Nadella, Lisa Su, Sergey Brin, and Musk on the ground floor of the Donald J. Trump Institute of Peace. The President had just arrived on site. The six of them would soon join him on stage to receive national medals of science or technology, but for now they were locked down in an adjoining auditorium with time to kill. “Okay, functional safety,” Huang soon said to the other five, apropos of nothing. “How does it work? An AI has a goal, how does it achieve it?” “By any means necessary,” Musk replied, laughing. Several layers of the Secret Service had temporarily separated these executives—who between them own or control companies worth around $18 trillion—from their security details and staff, their families and guests. Michael Kratsios, Trump’s chief scientific advisor and the man responsible for assembling them, had been called away by an aide to see his boss. After he left, the gang of six were left all but alone. There were two men from the White House video team on the dais, to whom each of the medalists was speaking in turn. While Huang talked to them, the conversation on the floor turned to compute. It was, to the benefit of Nvidia’s CEO, in short supply. “[Greg] Brockman at dinner was hounding me for compute,” Musk said, referring to OpenAI’s president. “He was asking me for compute,” Sergey Brin said. Musk marveled at his sense of the man’s chutzpah. “Dude, you stole my charity! You can’t be a huge dick then ask for favors, hello?” Brockman had famously kept a diary during the 2010s, which became relevant in court when Musk began his unsuccessful lawsuit against Sam Altman, OpenAI’s CEO, in 2024. “How many grown men do you know that keep a diary?” Brin said, throwing a log on the pyre. “If I did I’d burn it.” The current widespread lack of compute was nothing compared to the lack of memory chips. “I’ve never in my life seen a supply chain price shock like it,” Musk told the group, in disbelief at Micron’s 87 percent gross margin this past quarter, which has more than doubled in two years. (The company had booked $85 billion in net profit in the past 12 months.) Only six American companies had made more; half of them were run by men in the room. “They’re not really putting the money back,” Nadella said of Micron’s capex plans, sharing Musk’s skepticism of its desire to expand capacity fast. Stripped of their retinues and the gaze that follows them in any room, they were—once Huang rejoined them—just six people, standing in a circle. As in any circle, a dynamic soon became clear. Huang took the lead, but Musk, holding a small wine glass filled with Diet Coke and ice, was irrepressible and dominant. Su was quiet. She had initially stood off to the side, before Nadella peeled off from the main group to join her. Dell, whose eponymous company had at the time increased in value more than fivefold since February, seemed content to let others speak. Brin and Nadella served as conversational foils for Huang and Musk. “NetJets sucks for international travel,” Huang said, moving on to lighter matters. Musk turned to Dell. “He probably owns a fleet [of planes],” he said, smiling. “Just one,” replied Dell, tall, broad, and unhurried. “You can only be on one.” He credited Musk for creating Starlink. “I do Zoom meetings all the time.” “Starlink’s been great for us,” said Brin. Both men have owned a Gulfstream 650ER, which seats up to 19 people. Huang chooses not to own a jet, despite being trapped on a recent Delta flight without working Wi-Fi. “I sat quietly,” he said, which was hard to imagine; few men possess more compressed energy. “I read about 7,000 emails… Nothing drives me nuttier than not getting internet access. I’ve got work to do!” “Best way to sandbox an AI,” said Musk. “Put it on a Delta flight: No escape is possible.” They had all initially gathered with their entourages in another room down the hall. Musk brought his mother and three of his children; Huang brought his wife, adult children, and his parents; Su brought her husband; Brin brought his girlfriend, GiGi, a wellness influencer beloved by Trump; Dell and Nadella came alone. Musk, the only guest not to be screened by security, had bounded into that room last: wide-eyed, bigger than everyone else, already amused, not entirely in control of his movements. He had looked around with a teenager’s excitement at the 20 or so people present—in a room containing the U.S. secretary of energy, the administrator of NASA, and three of the 10 richest men in the world after himself—and had, within a minute, pulled out his phone to show a gaggle of them some test footage of the Tesla Roadster in flight. “This is meant to be top secret but whatever,” he said, smiling. Musk had been too absorbed by the footage to acknowledge Kratsios at first. (They know each other well.) Huang, capable of charming anyone, was more attentive, greeting Kratsios (“Director, nice to see you”) and making sure to introduce him to his parents as his father clasped Musk’s hand, beaming. “He is our nation’s chief scientist,” Huang told his parents of Kratsios, generously. He marveled at his youth. “39? I was at my peak at 39.” The medalists had then moved to this room to make way for POTUS and the phalanx that always surrounds him. The ground floor was cleared and refilled while the gang of six passed the time. An aide arrived in the doorway. The President was here. He was perhaps eight meters away, but quite unreachable. He then greeted the medalists one by one behind the stage. He shook hands, embraced them, left no shoulder untapped. When it came to Brin, Trump gave him a hug of sorts, gripping Brin by his arms as he motioned from side to side. “We love you,” Trump’s lips read, as he pulled back. Seven members of the Secret Service Assault Team, bearing automatic rifles and covered in tactical gear, filed into the auditorium vacated by the medalists as the action moved to the stage, where the President was flanked by more classically dressed agents. Trump spoke first, running through the achievements of each winner. He chose to start with and dwell longest on Musk, with whom his bond seemed stronger than ever. SpaceX had, that morning, safely returned four astronauts to Earth after eight months on board the International Space Station. “Could you imagine if things didn’t work out so well?” Trump said, veering off script. “I wonder if he’d be here… but it always works out well for Elon, right?” Less than 18 months earlier, Musk had taken to X to expose Trump’s presence in the Epstein files. (“Time to drop the really big bomb,” he wrote.) But something deeper than necessity had reconciled them. “We’re proud of you, very proud of you. National treasure,” Trump said on stage. Kratsios took to the lectern in front of a futuristic arching backdrop bearing the word SCIENCE, and proceeded to show a highly developed understanding of the President’s character. “Mr. President, before we get to the actual medaling, we have prepared a short video to celebrate the lifetime achievements of your uncle, a 1983 national medal of science recipient, John G. Trump.” Trump had already begun his remarks by invoking his uncle, an MIT professor for almost 40 years, whose intellect he never tires of mentioning. Kratsios had reached out to Brett Ratner, who has become Trumpworld’s in-house director since making Melania earlier this year, to help make the video. “Some scientists transform medicine. Some help win wars. John G. Trump did both,” it began. Kratsios sprung another surprise once it concluded, bringing out John G. Trump’s medal in a frame. He presented it to Trump, who gladly paraded it to the audience. The medalists duly made their way to the stage. “This is it, this is the whole ballgame,” Trump said to the recipients as he finished his remarks, enjoying the magnitude of the moment. “It is about time you were recognized. You are about to go down in the annals of history.” I caught up with Kratsios after the event. “The President’s excited,” he said, excited himself. Trump had felt the meaning of it all, Kratsios suggested, because of his uncle. “He loved it. He said, ‘Get me five more [names]. Let’s do another one.’” PHOTO BY BLUEEE / ALAMY President Trump applauds National Medal of Technology and Innovation recipients Satya Nadella, Michael Dell, Lisa Su, Elon Musk, Jensen Huang, and Sergey Brin during the “A New Golden Age” summit in Washington, D.C., October 8, 2026. Michael Kratsios has worked for Trump every day in office since January 20, 2017. He was little known in the first Trump term, but he has now become one of the few White House aides entrusted with making presidential caprice a reality. He has spent six years turning the traditionally irrelevant office he runs—the Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP)—into a consequential engine room of government. OSTP has historically been maligned for producing little more than congressionally mandated reports on, say, algae bloom. But Kratsios is using it to set tech policy across much of the U.S. government. He sits between the two most powerful constituencies in America—POTUS and Silicon Valley—and now effectively serves as the White House coordinator for critical emerging technologies, including in science, space, nuclear, and quantum. He is one of a handful of players steering AI policy for Trump, insofar as anyone has latitude to act on an issue the President has commandeered. Kratsios had watched Trump’s victory speech on the night of the 2016 election from the sunken trading floor at Thiel Capital in San Francisco, a day after turning 30. He had worked for Peter Thiel for six years by then, and knew he was witnessing a miraculous opportunity materialize in front of him. His boss, the first man in the Valley to back Trump, was about to be named to the transition’s executive committee. As an 18-year-old in 2005, Kratsios had worked as an intern in Lindsey Graham’s office during the summer of John Roberts’ Supreme Court confirmation. He briefly began his career in investment banking before landing with Thiel, but he had always wanted to return to D.C. He flew with Thiel and a handful of others to Trump Tower on the Monday after the election. They were given desks on the 14th floor, where he began to think through what a tech agenda could look like for the President, whose campaign had focused on more emotive issues like immigration, trade, and war. He helped organize the first meeting between Trump and the tech leaders of the day. (“You’ll call my people, you’ll call me, it doesn’t make any difference. We have no formal chain of command around here,” Trump told them then, before anyone realized how true that was.) When Thiel flew back to San Francisco, Kratsios stayed, and began to research the many offices and agencies of the federal government. He alighted on one: OSTP. This underutilized office in the White House, he thought, could become the most important office for science and technology in America. He couldn’t understand why no one else grasped its potential relevance. Every previous director had been a PhD scientist, focused on providing largely ceremonial scientific counsel that often went unheeded. Congress formally created the position in 1976 after Nixon, tired of being lectured by the scientific community over foreign policy, had dissolved an earlier iteration of the office. Congress’ aim was to ensure presidents received non-partisan advice, but its director was also in charge of an organ of government, and few scientists were naturally suited to the work of a bureaucrat. OSTP had, in Kratsios’ mind, long since turned inward. Its aims under Obama, he felt, over-indexed on climate science and fixing government websites—noble causes, but Kratsios traced OSTP’s lineage back to a much grander past: the wartime office run by a former MIT scientist, Vannevar Bush, that inaugurated the Manhattan Project. In its modern form, OSTP lacked formal authority over the agencies that spent $200 billion of America’s R&D dollars every year: the then-Department of Defense; the Department of Energy (DOE), which ran America’s 17 national labs; the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Science Foundation (NSF), the twin pillars of basic science research; and NASA. But it was a wing of the White House: it could command the federal bureaucracy in the president’s voice, so long as the president and chief of staff wanted it to. There was a chance Trump would shut it down. The Heritage Foundation wanted him to, and Obama had loved it, which might have been cause enough for the President-elect. But the Trump 45 White House had more important fights. OSTP was simply neglected instead, allowing Kratsios to get himself appointed as America’s deputy chief technology officer, housed inside the office. It was a role requiring no Senate confirmation, allowing him to start work immediately, and there was no CTO or OSTP director. The office was his. On January 21, 2017, Kratsios made his way through the Washington rain to the Eisenhower Executive Office Building (EEOB), the neighboring building that houses most White House staff. He had never been inside. A conference room full of civil servants were waiting for him on the fourth floor in fear of their jobs, at the end of a long checkered stone hallway. Kratsios, who is wiry, alert, and unlikely to berate anyone, moved into the room to introduce himself. He was a marathon runner, and a four-time winner of the Model UN competition at his South Carolina public school. As a 10-year-old boy on holiday in Japan in 1997 with his first and second-generation Greek immigrant parents, he had insisted on being taken to visit the Nozomi 500, the fastest train in the world. He was, to his great regret, too young to catch a flight on Concorde before it was decommissioned when he was 16. Now he wanted to bring it back, and turn OSTP into something more like an Office for the American Frontier. Trump was in the process of sending vandals into key government departments, as he would do again eight years later. Kratsios wasn’t one of them, but the civil servants in the conference room didn’t know that. “Hey, I’m Michael,” Kratsios said in his diffident way. I’m going to be working here. He met the two primary lifers in the office, and got to work. The President doesn’t leave much wall space to chance inside the West Wing. Every available inch of white paint running down the surprisingly low-ceilinged corridors of the White House has been covered by portraits of the man in action, whether disembarking Marine One, greeting a UFC fighter at the edge of the Octagon assembled in his honor this summer on the South Lawn, or striding out of an AI-generated wall of fire in his familiar get-up of box-cut suit, red tie, long black overcoat, and scowl fit for a mug shot. A marine stood guard at the entrance at noon on September 15, 2026, which meant the President was inside on the day that I was shown around by Kratsios. It was three weeks before the science summit-slash-medal ceremony. After a hushed tour, I stepped outside onto the gilded “Presidential Walk of Fame” installed by Trump along the building’s west colonnade, with its narrative history of each presidency, and stood beside the portrait of an autopen that depicts Joe Biden. Kratsios asked me if I wanted a picture. Trump would show off the pen to an unusually amused Xi Jinping nine days later. (“Sleepy Joe Biden was, by far, the worst President in American History…,” Trump writes of the only person to beat him in a presidential election.) To the left, chairs had been laid out for a press conference on the Rose Garden patio, paved over by Trump last summer. High heels no longer get caught in the grass, I was told. I looked out at the newly built helicopter pad behind the patio, and at the President’s half-built East Wing ballroom beyond that. I arrived at the White House unsure of how Kratsios wielded power in the office he had first identified as the outlet fit for his ambition almost a decade ago. AI had overwhelmed our conversation that morning: we were a day removed from Trump having called Jensen Huang at a conference to tell the world that Dario Amodei needed to shut his mouth—that AI safety fears were a hoax. “It’s almost a conspiracy,” the President told Huang on speakerphone in his wistful way, speaking as usual more to himself than anyone else. I wanted to understand what Kratsios was doing with the power he had won, how much the fight over AI was being resolved by his office, and how he operated under a President who valued the advice of capitalism’s most eminent men far more than the counsel offered by his staff. Kratsios’ appointment as OSTP director and presidential science advisor (the roles are paired) had been greeted in The New York Times as “an utter disaster” by one physics professor from the City College of New York, who declared: “Climate science is dead. God knows what’s going to happen to biomedicine. This marks the beginning of the decline of the golden age of American science.” I knew Kratsios was being mistaken with his patrons, past and present. Thiel had indeed tried to get one of America’s leading climate skeptics appointed as Trump’s science advisor in 2017. But ask pillars of official Washington, including former Biden appointees, and they would cast Kratsios as an almost non-partisan devotee of “progress studies.” He was not Russ Vought, the director of Office of Management and Budget, who was behind a Trump administration budget request that had sought to cut non-defense R&D spending by a third in 2026. Fortunately for Kratsios, Congress set U.S. science funding and paid the requests little heed, although Vought’s office could still slow-walk disbursements, as they have done. That was a constraint Kratsios faced rather than chose. One of Kratsios’ young staff would describe him to me in high school terms as “a geek who’s done well.” As Sihao Huang, the head of frontier compute strategy at Anthropic—who was until June Kratsios’ lead advisor on AI—put it to me, OSTP under Kratsios is a “group of nerds in the White House: a bunch of us engineers and physicists who would just stay in the building until like midnight, and… talk about neutrino dynamics.” “Michael personally has such a preference for people of STEM backgrounds,” Huang said. “I brought so many candidates in for him to interview, and he’s like, ‘Oh, this person is not technical enough, they don’t know what they’re talking about on AI.’ I’m like, ‘Michael, you have a degree in [politics, with a certificate in] Hellenic studies.’ He would send me obscure AI technical blogs [and ask], ‘What do you think about this particular benchmark of this Chinese open-source model and what this says about reinforcement learning on cyber capabilities?’” Kratsios had given me a sense that morning of what working for the President entailed. He had proposed a new space transportation policy to Trump in the Oval Office in August. Trump asked what Musk thought of it. Kratsios hadn’t shown Musk the specifics, so the President called him on the fly and had Kratsios brief him on speaker. “We have a little back and forth and then that call ends, and the President’s like, ‘Get Jeff on the phone.’” Kratsios duly briefed him next, winning Bezos’ approval and, with it, Trump’s signature. It was an evolution of the typical process described to me by a former White House official who worked for Trump in his first term: “Obama wanted to be, and often was, the smartest guy in the room. He’d read everything. Reagan hated dissent, and wanted his advisors to arrive with recommendations agreed in advance. Trump wants to hear and watch the debate in front of him. He’s not a reader of background papers, but he reads the room.” That room is not bound by the people in it. You don’t need to work in the West Wing to be the loudest voice heard by the President, who believes in social proof measured in dollars. And there’s no real way of knowing who he may listen to at any time. One government official who has worked closely with the Trump 47 White House likened the flow of power within it to the way light passes through a prism. “It’s like a many-sided object. On a particular day, the light will flow through a particular facet of that object. On another day, the light comes in at a different angle.” Kratsios has persisted by accepting his position in the White House’s hierarchy. The criticism you hear, insofar as it’s leveled, is that Kratsios is cautious to a fault with the President, and offers too few perspectives of his own. But that mistakes him for someone who thinks he has political capital to spend. “The frontmen tend to come and go, they run hot and cold,” as the former Trump 45 official puts it. “The people in the background survive. They get stuff done.” In all the major AI policy decisions of Trump’s term, Sihao Huang claimed, Kratsios has been the staffer who “stays in the room, and after a big decision is made one way or the other, he’s the one that actually writes the policy.” OSTP frequently drafts the Executive Orders (EOs) through which Trump directs the federal bureaucracy to enact science or tech policy, and Kratsios knows much more about the decrees being signed than the President does, which makes him seem vital. But I still wasn’t sure, when I spoke to Kratsios at the EEOB, whether holding the President’s pen amounts to glorified note-taking or the essential administrative act. The duality of Kratsios’ role was emphasized two weeks after my visit, when the President gathered everyone who mattered in AI for the White House Accord on Superintelligence. Kratsios was present, seated one in from the end of the table, and he was part of the group that decamped to the East Room to sign it with the heads of the frontier labs. But the eventual Executive Order he was responsible for writing called for no more than the renaming of AI to SI. The Accord itself—drafted by Zuckerberg, and shared with Kratsios the night before the summit—was, as one recent Trump aide suggested to me, an attempt to make it look like the White House was doing something about AI safety, rather than an attempt to actually do something about AI safety. Kratsios had indicated as much to me when we spoke in his offices inside the EEOB: it wasn’t for the government to act. “What does he [Amodei] want the government to do that they’re not doing? Do they [Anthropic] want us to uncover problems with his model that he has neglected to uncover himself? That’s what confuses me. Just announce tomorrow that you’re spending a billion dollars on safety… You control what training runs you’re doing. You control what guardrails you’re implementing. You control what the sandbox test environment looks like. You control how many third-party evaluation firms you engage with to test your model in advance. You control how many red teamers you hire. You control whether or not 90% of your engineers are working on engineering the frontier, or you take 20% of them to work on guardrails. That has nothing to do with the government.” I knew he appreciated a deeper set of arguments than the ones he was making that day. We had spoken earlier in the summer, when he had drafted an Executive Order inspired by Demis Hassabis’ proposal for AI companies to self-regulate under the imprimatur of the U.S. government (to stave off other international regulations). The AI accelerationists—Zuckerberg, Huang, and Trump’s former AI czar David Sacks, with whom Kratsios co-chairs the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology (PCAST)—had lobbied hard against it, and Trump was instinctively against it. “There are a lot of people who have a vested interest in absolutely nothing happening. There’s a lot of jockeying here,” as one official with knowledge of White House discussions put it to me. Since June 2, the frontier labs had, under White House pressure, been voluntarily sharing their models with various wings of the U.S. government 30 days before releasing them. The government, Kratsios told me in August, was fortunate only two companies were operating at the frontier, and releasing their most potent models at a tolerable cadence. But soon more companies would join the frontier, as they since have, and model release would speed up. What then? Kratsios had to quiet his own concerns: Trump’s clash with Amodei had set a new mood. “The people who are ‘sounding the alarm’ are literally the only ones that can solve the problem,” Kratsios duly told me when we spoke at the White House. “And rather than solving it, they just dump it on other people without any detail… I just don’t think they are aware enough to understand that the solution to all their problems is not Chuck Schumer.” In the aftermath of the Accord, Kratsios’ focus turned to his upcoming science summit. Stripe CEO Patrick Collison and U.S. secretary of energy Chris Wright would speak, along with NASA administrator Jared Isaacman, who was effusive about Kratsios’ ability to get agencies to work together. “There is no NASA-only,” he told me via video call from his car. “Putting a fission reactor in space [as the Trump administration has committed to doing by 2028] requires contributions from the Department of Energy, the Department of Transportation, there’s FAA [Federal Aviation Administration]. OSTP coordinates across all the technology and science leaders… It’s been an absolute pleasure to serve under Director Kratsios’ leadership.” But was there a better way to get the President to care about science than to talk about it? As the summit approached, Kratsios dreamt up the idea of presenting national medals to the men whose wealth, power, and perceived fealty have won Trump’s respect—while also, crucially, presenting one to the President himself. Two days before the summit , I had spoken to Kratsios late at night by phone. It was our fourth conversation; this one was different. He spoke frankly to me, like we knew each other and were having dinner. I felt he was walking me through the reality of his job at last, and explaining why he had first chosen and since stuck with OSTP. “In the Obama administration, a lot of tech coordination was haphazard and not centralized,” he said. “OSTP would never be the focal point of everything. The biggest takeaway that all the old Obama people had—and they were obsessed with this; they’d always use the same term—they said ‘seat at the table.’ That was all they thought. That’s the most important thing that you need to ensure. You need to go talk to the chief of staff, and make sure that happens: that OSTP has a seat at the table. “That is the least ambitious goal you can imagine!” he marveled. “That’s the saddest existence, where you’re begging to just be involved so you can add some kind of context as other people are making decisions. No—you need to be the one who calls the meeting. You need to be the one that’s driving the agenda. You guys are not thinking big enough. You need to have an opinion about where the nation needs to go on these big science and technology issues, and bring other people along. They shouldn’t be bringing you along. It’s the other way around.” The vision Kratsios was describing for the Office had been theorized for the first time in 1993, when Clinton put the OSTP director in operational control of a nominal National Science and Technology Council, but the body never had any weight when run by professional scientists. They were too disconnected from the source of their relevance: the West Wing. Kratsios’ inspiration, Vannevar Bush, understood that wellspring of his power when he ran a proto-OSTP under Franklin Roosevelt. “I knew that you couldn’t get anything done in that damn town,” Bush later told an interviewer, “unless you organized under the wing of the president.” Still, how did Kratsios, a political novice on arrival, work out how to get anything done? “First, you have to figure out what the policy action is you want to take, or the big initiative you want to drive, and make sure that you deeply understand and can articulate it in a lot of excruciating detail, with a lot of well-researched arguments as to why it’s the best thing for the country, why it’s the right thing for whatever topic you’re working on, why it politically makes sense for what the administration is trying to do. So you start with that, and that’s something you’ve got to do before you even start talking to anyone. “Then the next step is you have to map out who the most important players across the administration are, that are necessary to have on board. Then, before you even call any meetings, you have to go build support among the community [the relevant agencies] that you’re ultimately going to be tasking to do something.” PHOTO BY SMITH COLLECTION/GADO VIA GETTY IMAGES Leaders of the S-1 project debate the feasibility of a 184-inch cyclotron in Berkeley, California on March 29, 1940 (left to right): nuclear scientist E.O. Lawrence, physicist Arthur Compton, engineer Vannevar Bush, chemist James B. Constant, physicist Karl Compton, and physicist Alfred Loomis. I’d come to think of Kratsios as like a plumber for America’s most vital drains, unblocking the barriers to innovation across any area of national interest: nuclear energy, supersonic travel, space policy, quantum computing. Yet he knew that everything he directed agencies to do in Trump’s name could be rescinded on January 20, 2029. His work would only last if he enacted changes his successor wouldn’t want to reverse. “There’s one type of EO that says, you know, this type of activity in the energy industry is now allowed, and then when the administration flips, [it] is no longer allowed. What I like to spend time on [instead] is the type of EOs that essentially spurred the entire nuclear renaissance that we’re experiencing today.” In June and July, four new privately run nuclear reactors achieved “criticality” (a self-sustaining nuclear reaction) under a new DOE pilot program. That did not amount to a nuclear renaissance, exactly, but it exceeded a target of three set by Kratsios in a May 2025 EO signed by Trump. “I’d always thought that it was insane we didn’t have more nuclear energy,” he told me, dating his ambition to revive the industry back to Thiel’s 2011 National Review essay, “The End of the Future.” (He had read it as a 24-year-old analyst, in his second year working for Thiel.) The success of the initiative had produced many fathers, with most of the focus on those inside DOE. That was the strange fact of Kratsios’ job: it was unglamorous and often uncredited, but done well it could provoke some lasting change. It was toil fit for a technocrat. You had to value the work itself. “The rules at the NRC [Nuclear Regulatory Commission] will change. They will change. You’re not rolling those back, and at that point you’re going to have a bunch of different reactors in the pipeline for approval. I mean, you can’t pull it back.” The people who are ‘sounding the alarm’ are literally the only ones that can solve the problem. And rather than solving it, they just dump it on other people without any detail… I just don’t think they are aware enough to understand that the solution to all their problems is not Chuck Schumer. He was excited to think back to how much more he could do now than he had done in Trump’s first term. Back then, American companies were having to go to Rwanda to test drone prototypes. Changing that was one of the few achievements of those early years. “You’re sitting at your desk, and you’re like, ‘You know, it really sucks that commercial drone operations aren’t happening. And the only people at fault for this are the U.S. government.’” So you go to the FAA, he told me, and they’re willing to change the policy, but then the security people won’t be happy if drones fly anywhere near their facilities, so then you have to talk to the FBI, and the Department of War, and the Department of Energy, which runs the nuclear sites. That was a simple shift, and even that involved corralling all of government. This stuff scales, he assured me. Once you got the hang of it, there was no limit to how big you could dream. His work was of a different order now. Earlier this year, he had shepherded the so-called “ratepayer protection pledge” into existence, getting the President to announce it in the State of the Union, and since signing up hundreds of companies to a voluntary commitment to build, buy, or bring the power they need for data centers. The Speaker of the House had taken the policy up. But science was the terrain that excited Kratsios most. That began with “Genesis,” the latest government program to be fatefully cast as the next Manhattan Project. It consisted of a centralized platform through which any federally funded scientist would be able to access both compute and deep government datasets to advance their experiments. Kratsios had, by the time of the summit, pushed the biggest players in industry—Nvidia, AMD, Google, Amazon, Anthropic, and Open AI—to donate $2.4 billion in compute as part of the plan. Executives from each of the firms stood on a crowded stage on the day itself and duly announced their number, giving the occasion the appearance of a shakedown. “Imagine you’re a researcher and you can’t access this compute. Who has your back? We do. We’re trying to get them billions in free compute,” Kratsios told me animatedly that night. “No one else can say, ‘Hey can we have a billion of free compute?’ and it just happen! It’s the White House having an opinion. Everything we’re doing is a partnership between government, philanthropy, and the private sector—that’s what makes it last.” Kratsios’ zeal would ring hollow, however, to anyone who judged federal support for science by the size of the scientific bureaucracy. Although total grant spending at NIH has not fallen compared to the Biden years, staffing levels are, since Trump’s return, down by 35 percent at NSF, the primary funder of basic research at U.S. universities (after NIH, its bigger biomedical sister). Members of Kratsios’ team welcomed the downsizing as an opportunity to reshape the institution, but it also inevitably left a vocal chunk of the academic science community in despair. I missed much of the summit’s onstage program. The real action was taking place backstage, but the ideas being expressed by the speakers were clear enough. The most fundamental of them was an embrace of metascience: the act of applying the scientific method to the scientific enterprise. This was strangely absent from the current approach at NIH and NSF, which scarcely tracked the productivity of their grant-making practices. “Metascience in government has typically been done by funding external examiners,” Caleb Watney, a co-founder of the DC-based Institute for Progress, had explained to me. “But the only entity that has the sample size to run accurate experiments is the federal government.” Kratsios’ accompanying report had explained how metascience units would be given “the authority to run experiments and compel program officers to participate,” to avoid these new teams devolving into little more than compliance operations. Without metascience you couldn’t test any of the other ideas it outlined: giving more money directly to scientists rather than for specific projects, speeding up grant applications and approvals, circumventing the conformity of peer review, establishing a broader array of research institutions, and funding young scientists in America—Kratsios’ most impassioned plea. In 1983, 18 percent of NIH’s main research grants went to lead scientists aged 36 and under. By 2010, only three percent did. The median age of first-time NIH grant recipients is now 42. “We have abandoned young scientists in America!” Kratsios claimed. “These are issues that are just not on the radar. This is the seed corn for the future of this country.” You could trace Kratsios’ ideas back through time. They were born out of arguments long made by Thiel himself, who had criticized “the way that higher education institutions distort grant-making processes, and values, and the search for truth,” as Sihao Huang had put it. They also answered Patrick Collison’s call eight years ago in The Atlantic for “a large-scale institutional response” to the growing inefficiency of scientific research. (The pair are close. Collison had recently come to dinner at Kratsios’ home to offer advice to a handful of aligned officials across government.) And there was Kratsios’ own story, which tracked back to the 10 year old who had insisted his parents let him catch a train from Hiroshima to Tokyo so that he could ride the fastest train in the world. Why should science stagnate, not least now that superintelligence was here? It should speed up. Kratsios’ bid for scientific revolution was also not quite as novel as it seemed. Every generation or so since the Civil War, the government and the scientific establishment had fought over who was in control of whom. A lot of the fears and hopes and tensions playing out now in the Silicon Age played out first in the Industrial and Atomic Ages. Thiel had fueled the latest iteration of this periodic wave. Kratsios was the guy who got himself appointed and, eventually, congressionally approved in Trump’s first term. There are other sons of Peter in government now—Emil Michael at the Department of War, Jay Bhattacharya at NIH, and Jim O’Neill, nominated to lead NSF—but Kratsios was the one in the White House. He had taken a set of Thielian ideas for government and was attempting to actually enact them. He has a stamina that Thiel lacked for the fight, as his mentor admits. Reached for comment on his former chief of staff, Thiel told Colossus : “I do not have the extraordinary patience nor pain tolerance to work in politics. Every American should be grateful that someone of Michael’s caliber does.” Musk didn’t have the patience for it either. Few do. It’s the work of a marathon runner. Kratsios has grown up in office, worked out how to make certain things happen, and done it under the most capricious president in modern history. He was dismissed as “an inoffensive bureaucrat” in one book written on Thiel in 2021, and deemed to be an inconsequential person to have made it through the transition and into the West Wing. But that was a virtue. To carry out Thielian political ideas in practice, it pays to be an inoffensive bureaucrat, as long as you’re an industrious and effective one. Few institutions react well to being told they’re going to be flayed alive. Harry Lambert is a reporter based in London.
